sentences.t: By 1983, Philips had spent five years failing to sell its wafer stepper.

The PAS 2000 - a machine that prints circuit patterns onto silicon - had been kept alive in a corner of the Dutch conglomerate on a manager's discretionary budget, and its 50 engineers needed 120 million guilders the company would not spend.
Philips went to the lithography market leader, Perkin Elmer, and offered a partnership.
Perkin Elmer chose a Liechtenstein startup instead (ASML's own founding account).

So Philips settled for Arthur del Prado, founder of ASM International - the first Dutchman to take a company onto the Nasdaq - and on April 1, 1984 the two opened ASM Lithography in a leaky shed beside a Philips office in Eindhoven.
Forty-seven of the fifty engineers signed on; many considered the venture asset stripping.
Their product was a stepper whose hydraulic wafer stage - oil, in a cleanroom - everyone already knew was obsolete.
The shed, the reluctant staff and the compromised machine: that was the entire inheritance.
Four years in, the company was dying.

It had few customers in a market full of suppliers; shareholder ASM International, bleeding money, withdrew; the global electronics industry turned down; and Philips announced a vast cost-cutting program.

The young company, in ASML's own telling, hung in the balance - until its executives reached Philips board member Henk Bodt, who persuaded his colleagues to lend a final helping hand (ASML's history).
The loan was put into one machine.
In 1991 the company launched the PAS 5500 - a platform with the productivity and resolution to win the customers that finally made it profitable - and in 1995 ASML listed in Amsterdam and New York.
Philips sold half its stake at the IPO and the rest over the following years.
The unwanted division was now on its own, solvent, and about to make the most expensive bet in its industry's history.
By 1994-95, ASML's technologists had concluded that the industry's workhorse - deep ultraviolet light at 193 nanometers - would eventually stop shrinking chips.

Martin van den Brink, who had led the PAS 5500 and would become president and CTO, championed an absurd alternative: extreme ultraviolet light at 13.5 nanometers, a wavelength that passes through neither air nor glass.

He put a senior manager named Jos Benschop in charge, and in 1998 ASML and lens-maker Carl Zeiss formed a European consortium to chase it (Michael Cusumano's account in the Communications of the ACM).
In 2000 a small team started a prototype.
It took six years.

The light itself had to be invented as an industrial tool: lasers striking molten droplets of tin tens of thousands of times a second to make plasma that glows at 13.5 nanometers, reflected - nothing can be refracted - by mirrors polished to sub-nanometer precision.
The final bill ran to roughly two decades and about $11 billion of R&D, coordinated by one firm (Cusumano).
No customer asked for this.
ASML decided the physics was inevitable and spent accordingly.
By 2012 the bet was visibly working and visibly unaffordable, so ASML did something no equipment maker had done: it asked its customers to buy the company.
Intel took 15% for about $4 billion; TSMC and Samsung took smaller stakes - the three biggest chipmakers on earth paying in advance for a machine that did not yet exist in production form.
In 2013 ASML bought Cymer, the San Diego light-source maker, to own the hardest part of EUV outright (the company timeline).

The first EUV prototype had shipped to a research customer in 2010; the production-ready NXE:3400 won batch orders in 2016; by 2020 EUV was in high-volume manufacturing and ASML shipped its hundredth system.

The customers who funded the machine became its hostages and its beneficiaries at once: TSMC rode EUV to a manufacturing lead that Intel, which delayed adopting it until 2025, is still trying to recover from (Cusumano).
What the bet bought: roughly 90% of the world's lithography tools and 100% of the EUV kind.
Each machine weighs about 400,000 pounds - the size of a double-decker bus - travels in three Boeing 747s, and contains more than 100,000 modules from some 800 suppliers.
The ordinary versions cost around $200 million; the newest, for the densest chips, around $400 million (Cusumano).
Nikon and Canon, the duopoly ASML once chased, gave up on EUV entirely.

The monopoly is not one invention but the integration itself: light source, optics, mask, wafer stage and software from hundreds of specialist firms, all functioning as one vacuum-sealed system under extreme thermal and mechanical constraints.
Copying any component is possible; copying the coordination has so far proven to be the actual moat.
ASML is Europe's most valuable technology company - worth about $677 billion by Cusumano's September tally, and about 482 billion euros as of Wednesday's close (market data).
Since 2019, following US policy, the Netherlands has barred ASML's most advanced machines from China, and later extended the ban to the latest DUV systems.

Beijing's answer, as Reuters has reported: a state-overseen project with Huawei as system integrator, which by early 2025 had former ASML engineers running a prototype in a Shenzhen laboratory built partly from secondhand ASML components.
Observers put commercial Chinese EUV at 2030 or later - and the target moves while they chase it (Cusumano).
The target now is High NA: the EXE platform, shipped from 2023, raising the numerical aperture to 0.55.

In June this year MIT Technology Review's Clive Thompson climbed one with Jos Benschop - the same Benschop van den Brink picked in the 1990s - 150 tons of precision aluminum, 200-plus cubic meters of mechatronics holding mirrors with atomic precision, priced around $400 million.
Even Benschop, twenty years into building them, told Thompson he sometimes looks at the machine and goes: oh my God (Technology Review).

This October, ASML reported a record third quarter: €11.7 billion of net sales at a 57.5% gross margin, €5.0 billion of net income, 113 new systems sold - and said that its planned supply for both 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet customer demand (the Q3 release).
The company that sells the only machine is sold out through 2028.
Tonight in New York, Anthropic's $81.3 billion debut prices demand for what the machine's output makes possible; the Fed's minutes, published the same week, ask who is financing it.
Both questions route through Veldhoven.
End where the bet was placed.

Some time in 1994 or 1995, Martin van den Brink looked at a light source that passed through nothing, that no supplier could build, that two decades and $11 billion would be needed to tame - and decided the physics was inevitable.
The shed company had one non-obvious asset: nothing to protect.
Perkin Elmer said no to the inheritance; Nikon and Canon said no to the light.
The monopoly that tonight's debut quietly depends on was assembled entirely from other people's refusals - and one company's yes.
